claims.text: The initial non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy has a metastable, supersaturated, predominantly solid-solution microstructure.
Mg is initially distributed homogeneously within the solid-solution matrix.
The alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
Exposure to corrosive environments or high-temperature oxidation conditions drives Mg diffusion out of the supersaturated matrix.
Diffusing Mg forms fine-scale Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The Mg-rich precipitates can form at grain boundaries or within grains.
Formation of Mg-rich precipitates depletes Mg from the remaining matrix.
Mg depletion changes the reactivity of the matrix.
Mg depletion and precipitate formation alter the kinetics, composition, morphology, and protective character of the surface oxide scale.
The altered oxide scale changes corrosion behavior.
The altered oxide scale changes high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Corrosion testing may use an ambient chloride-containing salt-spray environment with controlled salt concentration.
High-temperature oxidation testing may be conducted at 600–800 degrees Celsius under controlled conditions.
A homogenizing thermal treatment will remove supersaturation from the comparison samples.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, phase-separated material will show lower matrix Mg content and emergent Mg-rich precipitates.
The phase-separated material will have different corrosion and oxidation performance from the baseline, although the direction of change is unspecified.
Minor alloying elements and processing history can influence precipitate formation and functional properties.

A lack of significant differences in Mg distribution, precipitation, oxide-scale characteristics, corrosion, and oxidation behavior between metastable and homogenized samples would falsify the proposed mediation mechanism.
